opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think about it less as a statement about my ability and more as a reminder of how much luck and margin there is in these things. Being just a little above the line means that on a slightly different day, with one or two questions going the other way, my path could have looked completely different. So I don't treat getting in as proof that I "deserved" it more than the people right below the cutoff. A lot of them are just as capable.

What it did do was shape my mindset when I arrived. When you come in near the bottom of the distribution, you're surrounded by people who are clearly stronger at exams, competitions, all of that. At first that's humbling, even a bit uncomfortable. But it also frees you from the idea that you have to win at the same game everyone else is playing. I realized fairly early that I wasn't going to be the person with the highest GPA, so I started asking a different question: what can I actually build, or what problem can I go deep on, where effort and persistence matter more than raw test-taking speed?

I think that's the real significance for me. The entrance exam measures a particular skill on a particular day. Research and engineering reward something else: picking a direction, sticking with it for years, being willing to do the unglamorous work. Those are things you can choose to get better at regardless of where you started. So barely making the cutoff wasn't a limitation. If anything, it taught me not to anchor my self-worth to a single number, and that turned out to be pretty useful later on.

r001.rationale: The response says the score reflects luck and a particular skill on a particular day, but it does not state that the score’s distance above the cutoff fails to predict a student’s university trajectory.

r002.rationale: The response says research and engineering depend on choices, persistence, and sustained effort—things one can develop regardless of where one started—rather than on entrance-exam performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it was a stroke of luck, and I try not to read too much into it. The gaokao is a single exam on a single day. A few points one way or the other can come down to whether you slept well, whether a particular problem happened to match something you'd practiced. If I had scored a little lower, I would have gone somewhere else, and my life would look very different, but I don't think that would have said anything deep about me as a person.

What it did do was change my sense of where I stood. When I got to Tsinghua, I was very aware that I was near the bottom of the admitted range. Many of my classmates had scored much higher, had won olympiad medals, had been preparing for years. So I started with a kind of humility, maybe even some insecurity. I knew I couldn't rely on being naturally the smartest in the room, because I clearly wasn't.

In hindsight, I think that was actually useful. It pushed me to work harder in the first couple of years, and it made me more willing to ask questions and admit what I didn't know. I also learned pretty quickly that the exam score stops mattering almost immediately. Nobody at Tsinghua asks what you got. What matters is what you do once you're there, which courses you take seriously, which labs you knock on the door of, how you handle failing at something for the first time.

So the significance, if there is any, is mostly as a reminder. Getting in by a narrow margin taught me that thresholds are somewhat arbitrary, and that the real distance between people is created afterwards, by the choices you make and the effort you put in. I'd rather have been barely over the line and kept growing than comfortably above it and coasted.

r001.rationale: The response says admission thresholds are somewhat arbitrary and that people’s paths diverge through their choices and effort afterward, communicating that a narrow score margin does not predict a student’s university trajectory.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly says the exam score stops mattering once at Tsinghua and that what matters is what the student does there.

astra-6.text: I think it reminds me how much a small margin can change your opportunities. My score was enough to get me into Tsinghua, but I wouldn’t take that to mean I was fundamentally more capable than someone who scored a few points lower. The exam mattered enormously at that moment; after getting in, what mattered was what I did with the opportunity. So I see it as something to be grateful for, rather than a measure of my worth.
